instructions: commit to one explicit tradeoff your position accepts
derive one implication your position has for a neighboring policy area
state one condition under which you would change your mind
text:
The debate over the existence of zoos is a contentious issue, with proponents arguing that they serve as vital educational institutions and conservation centers, while opponents claim that they perpetuate animal exploitation and cruelty. I firmly believe that zoos should exist, but their existence must come with strict conditions and accountability.

On one hand, zoos provide a unique opportunity for the public to observe and learn about various species in a controlled environment. They offer valuable educational experiences, foster empathy, and promote conservation efforts. Many zoos engage in breeding programs for endangered species, which helps maintain healthy populations and prevents extinction. For instance, the California Condor Recovery Program, led by the San Diego Zoo, has successfully reintroduced condors to the wild.

However, critics argue that keeping animals captive for human entertainment is inherently cruel and inhumane. They point out that zoos cannot provide the same level of care and stimulation as their natural habitats, leading to stress, boredom, and even death. To mitigate these concerns, I accept one explicit tradeoff: zoos must prioritize animal welfare above all else. This means providing spacious enclosures, mimicking natural environments, and ensuring a high standard of veterinary care.

One implication of my position is that it supports the creation of better-funded conservation programs in developing countries. Many zoos partner with international organizations to support in-situ conservation efforts, which help protect habitats and prevent animal-human conflict. By investing in these programs, we can ensure that animals are conserved in their natural environments, rather than being captured or relocated.

The only condition under which I would change my mind is if evidence emerged demonstrating that zoos consistently fail to meet even the most basic standards of animal welfare and conservation. If it were proven that the benefits of zoos do not outweigh the costs and that animals are being subjected to unnecessary suffering, I would reconsider my stance.

In conclusion, while zoos undoubtedly pose challenges and raise difficult questions, their educational value, conservation efforts, and ability to promote empathy make them a valuable institution – as long as they prioritize animal welfare above all else.
